# What carries the signal

## Predictor weights by outcome

![](../../results/figures/protocol_v2/index_importance_top10_level.png){width="100%"}

::: {.notes}
The index is linear in the rank-normalised predictors, so its component weights project back exactly onto the `r Q$n_pred` columns (scripts 57 and 58). Shown: the ten largest weights in the pooled four-country fit on the biomarker level, coloured by data source; a star marks a sign not reproduced in every country's own fit. No predictor carries more than 2% of the index's variance; the satellite embedding, climate and soil together carry `r pc(Q$env_lo)` to `r pc(Q$env_hi)` depending on the outcome. Likely question: whether these are causes. They are not; the weights say where deficiency is. Livestock density carrying a positive sign for iron and B12 is ecological: pastoral zones are the dry, poor zones in these countries.
:::

## Malawi, women's B12: the weights behind the best ranking

![](`r file.path(FIG, "fig12_vim_forest_Malawi_women_b12_plain.png")`)

::: {.notes}
Malawi, women's B12, biomarker level: the cell with the best in-fill ranking of the 24 (Spearman 0.70; The Gambia child vitamin A is next at 0.69). The index is linear in the rank-normalised columns, so every column has a standardised weight in a fit; the twenty largest are shown. Intervals: the index was refitted on 300 bootstrap resamples of Malawi's 87 surveyed districts, with the domain components re-oriented and the weights re-learned each time; the bar is the 5th to 95th percentile and the hollow marker the weight in the full fit. Every one of the twenty keeps its sign in at least 95 percent of refits. The level target is the negated log concentration, so a positive weight means worse status. Read the signs as district-level associations in Malawi: districts where more infants are fed meat or fish, more households ate fish last week and the wealth score is higher have better B12 status, and districts that are poorer, grassier, further from permanent water and with more pigs have worse. The diet items point the way a nutritional story would expect; the anaemia and malaria surfaces run the other way (more anaemia and malaria, better B12), which is the lakeshore and the south against the uplands, and a reminder that these are ecological associations, not effects. Script: scripts/policy_deck/09_vim_forest_example.R, which takes any country, outcome and target through environment variables. B12 is measured in three of the four surveys, so this cell does not enter the cross-country transport figures.
:::

## A surrogate marker: anaemia, fish and B12

```{r b12-surrogate, fig.width=12, fig.height=5.2, dpi=130}
ok <- FALSE
try({
  suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(sf))
  source(file.path(root, "R", "protocol_v2.R"))
  S  <- read.csv(file.path(root, "data", "covariates", "harmonized", "predictors_admin2_shared.csv"), check.names = FALSE)
  PREDS <- intersect(MD$column, names(S)); domain_of <- stats::setNames(MD$domain, MD$column)
  B <- readRDS(file.path(root, "dashboard", "data", "admin2_boundaries.rds"))[["malawi"]]
  t <- TG[TG$country == "Malawi" & TG$outcome == "women_b12" & is.finite(TG$y_prev), c("Admin1", "Admin2", "y_prev")]
  s <- S[S$country == "Malawi", c("Admin1", "Admin2", "ihme_allanemia", "hces_any_fish", PREDS)]
  m <- dplyr::left_join(s, t, by = c("Admin1", "Admin2"))          # every district; y_prev NA where no survey clusters
  # the deployment fit: the index on all surveyed districts, applied to every district (as on the dashboard)
  tr <- which(is.finite(m$y_prev)); Xr <- prep_predictors_v2(as.matrix(m[, PREDS])); Y <- .v2_logit(m$y_prev)
  D <- domain_representation_v2(Xr, domain_of, sign_rows = tr)
  m$pred <- .v2_expit(ARMS_V2[["domain_index"]](tr, seq_len(nrow(m)), Y, NULL, D, list(Admin1 = m$Admin1, y_nat = Y)))
  g <- dplyr::left_join(B, m[, c("Admin1", "Admin2", "y_prev", "pred", "ihme_allanemia", "hces_any_fish")], by = c("Admin1", "Admin2"))
  r1 <- cor(g$y_prev, g$ihme_allanemia, method = "spearman", use = "complete.obs"); r2 <- cor(g$y_prev, g$hces_any_fish, method = "spearman", use = "complete.obs")
  pct <- function(x) 100 * (rank(x, na.last = "keep") - 1) / (sum(is.finite(x)) - 1)   # within-country percentile, so the maps share one scale
  labs4 <- c(y_prev = "Women's B12 deficiency\nsurvey 2015-16\n ", pred = "Model-predicted deficiency\nevery district, fitted on\nthe surveyed ones",
             ihme_allanemia = sprintf("Modelled anaemia\nin women (IHME)\nrho with B12 def. = %.2f", r1), hces_any_fish = sprintf("Households eating\nfish last week (IHS4)\nrho with B12 def. = %.2f", r2))
  long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(labs4), function(v) data.frame(g[, c("Admin1", "Admin2")], value = pct(g[[v]]), panel = labs4[[v]])))
  long$panel <- factor(long$panel, levels = labs4)
  print(ggplot(sf::st_as_sf(long)) + geom_sf(aes(fill = value), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.1) + facet_wrap(~ panel, ncol = 4) +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(na.value = "grey92", name = "Percentile among Malawi districts (100 = highest)", limits = c(0, 100)) +
    theme_void(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.key.width = grid::unit(1.6, "cm"), strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10, lineheight = 1.05), strip.clip = "off", panel.spacing.x = grid::unit(1.0, "cm")))
  ok <- TRUE
}, silent = TRUE)
if (!ok) cat("Maps could not be rendered in this session.")
```

::: {.notes}
The story behind the forest plot on the previous slide. In Malawi the modelled anaemia and malaria surfaces carry negative weights for B12: districts with MORE anaemia and malaria have BETTER B12 status. No nutritional mechanism says that. The maps say why: the lakeshore and the southern lowlands are where malaria transmission and anaemia are highest, and they are also where households eat fish, the main dietary B12 source in the country; the uplands have less malaria, less fish and worse B12. The anaemia surface is a surrogate marker for that geography, not a cause, and it is a good one precisely because it is modelled from the same environment. Three lessons for the audience: the index finds these markers on its own, they are ecological associations and must never be read as effects, and a surrogate that works in Malawi need not work in the next country, which is why the cross-border models lean on climate and soil rather than on health surfaces (ablation slide). The second panel is the deployment fit (the index fitted on the 87 surveyed districts and applied to all 243, in-sample for the surveyed ones, as on the dashboard): it fills the grey districts and smooths the survey's single-cluster noise, and it visibly follows the anaemia and fish geography. Each map is the within-country percentile of its variable so the four share one scale; rho is the Spearman correlation with B12 deficiency across the surveyed Traditional Authorities (negative for anaemia and for fish: more of either, less deficiency).
:::

## Domain ablation under transport

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="34%"}
Loss in transported Spearman (biomarker level, `r Q$tr_cells` cells) when each domain is dropped and the components rebuilt, mean over cells with a 95% interval. The load-bearing domains are `r paste(head(Q$da_top$domain, 3), collapse = ", ")`; removing `r Q$da_neg` of the `r Q$da_n` domains costs nothing or helps.
:::
::: {.column width="66%"}
```{r ablation, fig.width=5.8, fig.height=5.6, dpi=160}
if (!is.null(DA)) {
  d <- abl_delta(DA, "domain") |> filter(target == "level") |> cell_ci("delta", "domain") |> arrange(est) |> mutate(domain = factor(domain, levels = domain))
  forest(d, "domain", null = 0, base = 12, xlab = "Loss in transported Spearman when dropped (mean, 95% interval)")
}
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Positive values mean the domain is load-bearing. Climate and soil carry most, with the anaemia surfaces, agriculture and greenness behind; the water-and-sanitation, education and infant-feeding domains sit at or below zero: removing them does not hurt a new country and in two cases helps. The DHS-derived domains are not in the headline set at all: with them in, the district transport index scores `r f2(Q$tr_dhs)` against `r f2(Q$tr_index)` without. A fixed climate-and-soil index transports at `r f2(Q$cs_d)` at district level and `r f2(Q$cs_a1)` regionally against `r f2(Q$tr_index)` and `r f2(Q$tr_a1)` for the full vocabulary; it was found on the same four countries it is scored on and enters the next country as a pre-registered prediction.
:::

## What the transport models reach for

::: {.notes}
Source: results/tables/protocol_v2/index_importance_columns.csv, scope "loco": the index fitted on three countries, projected back to columns, for each of the `r Q$loco_fits` held-out country and outcome combinations on the biomarker level; a column counts once per fit in which it is among the twenty largest standardised weights. Every column named on the slide keeps the same sign in every fit where it appears (`r if (!is.null(REC)) sum(REC$sign_agree[REC$n_fits >= 5] == 1) else NA` of the `r if (!is.null(REC)) sum(REC$n_fits >= 5) else NA` columns that recur in five or more fits are unanimous). The pattern is the one on the previous two slides seen from the other side: what a model trained elsewhere reaches for in a new country is the physical environment and the modelled nutrition surfaces built from it, not the country's own survey items. The staple-price and malaria signs are worth saying aloud: relatively expensive staples mark market-integrated, better-off districts, and high malaria transmission marks the wet, productive lowlands where diets are more diverse; neither is a mechanism to act on.
:::

## Replicated indicators

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="34%"}
Indicators whose district-level association with the outcome has the same sign in every country with the outcome, ranked by pooled meta-analytic z. Positive z means more deficiency.
:::
::: {.column width="66%"}
```{r signal, fig.width=5.8, fig.height=5.2, dpi=160}
if (!is.null(SIG)) {
  d <- SIG[SIG$sign_agree >= SIG$k_countries & SIG$k_countries >= 3 & SIG$group %in% c("child_vitA", "child_iron", "women_iron", "women_vitA"), ]
  d <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(d, d$group), function(g) head(g[order(-abs(g$meta_z)), ], 4)))
  d$Outcome <- olab[d$group]; d$Direction <- ifelse(d$mu > 0, "More deficiency", "Less deficiency")
  d$key <- factor(paste(d$predictor, d$group), levels = paste(d$predictor, d$group)[order(d$group, d$meta_z)])
  ggplot(d, aes(meta_z, key, colour = Direction)) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey45") + geom_point(size = 3) +
    facet_wrap(~ Outcome, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) + scale_y_discrete(labels = function(k) sub(" [a-z_A-Z]+$", "", k)) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c("More deficiency" = "#b2182b", "Less deficiency" = "#2166ac")) +
    labs(x = "Pooled z (random-effects meta-analysis)", y = NULL, colour = NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
}
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Legume cultivation and cattle ownership track more deficiency at district level, the reverse of the household-level dietary relationship, which is an ecological-fallacy signature: the replicated axis is rural subsistence agro-ecology, useful for deciding where to look and uninformative about what to change. No malaria burden indicator replicates; child wasting tracks women's vitamin A deficiency in all four countries. An earlier version of these slides had the signs inverted.
:::

# Limits and survey design

## Reliability ceiling

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="34%"}
The correlation a perfect predictor of the true district prevalence could reach, given the survey's sampling noise, by country. The honest ceiling averages `r f2(Q$vc_honest)` against a split-half ceiling of `r f2(Q$vc_split)`; the index reaches its ceiling in `r Q$vc_at` of `r Q$vc_n` cells.
:::
::: {.column width="66%"}
```{r ceiling, fig.width=5.8, fig.height=4.2, dpi=160}
if (!is.null(VC)) {
  d <- VC |> filter(rung == "admin2", target == "prev") |> transmute(country, outcome, `Split-half ceiling` = ceiling_within_vc, `Honest ceiling` = ceiling_vc, `Achieved, in-fill` = achieved_spearman) |>
    pivot_longer(-c(country, outcome), names_to = "quantity", values_to = "v") |> group_by(country, quantity) |> summarise(v = mean(v, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(quantity = factor(quantity, levels = c("Split-half ceiling", "Honest ceiling", "Achieved, in-fill")), country = sub("SierraLeone", "Sierra Leone", country))
  ggplot(d, aes(v, country, colour = quantity, shape = quantity)) + geom_point(size = 3.5, position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c("Split-half ceiling" = "grey55", "Honest ceiling" = "#1f4e79", "Achieved, in-fill" = "#b15928")) +
    labs(x = "Spearman correlation (mean over outcomes)", y = NULL, colour = NULL, shape = NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = 13) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
}
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
A respondent-in-cluster-in-district-in-region variance model reproduces the split-half ceiling when the cluster is counted as geography, then removes the cluster term: `r pc(Q$vc_share)` of the split-half ceiling was cluster effect. Child zinc has no district geography; what looked like geography was the cluster, and the time of the blood draw explains part of the cluster effect (ZN-02).
:::

## Survey design: district error

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="34%"}
Median district error in percentage points against the share of a full survey sampled, four designs, `r Q$tr_cells` cells. At 5% of the sample a national anchor plus the transported ranking gives `r f2(Q$ar_a1, 1)` points, a regional survey `r f2(Q$ar_c, 1)` and a district survey `r f2(Q$ar_b, 1)`.
:::
::: {.column width="66%"}
```{r anchor, fig.width=5.8, fig.height=4.4, dpi=160}
if (!is.null(AR)) {
  lab <- c(A1_anchor_rank = "National anchor + ranking", A2_region_anchor_rank = "Regional anchors + ranking", B_district_survey = "District survey", C_regional_survey = "Regional survey")
  d <- AR |> filter(rank_from == "prev", set == "climate_soil", design %in% names(lab)) |> group_by(design, fraction) |>
    summarise(mae = median(mae, na.rm = TRUE), lo = quantile(mae, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE), hi = quantile(mae, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |> mutate(Design = lab[design])
  ggplot(d, aes(fraction, mae, colour = Design)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point(size = 2.5) + scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
    labs(x = "Share of the full survey sample", y = "Median district error (percentage points)", colour = NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = 13) + theme(legend.position = "bottom") + guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2))
}
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
A district survey matches the anchored ranking's level error at about `r pc(Q$ar_b_match)` of the full sample. The ranking wins on level error only: a district survey of any size captures more burden, because burden sits in populous districts that surveys measure precisely. Fitted symmetrically on a reduced survey, the model's error degrades in step with the survey's, so the model improves the ordering at any sample size and does not reduce the sample a survey needs.
:::

## Transport by number of training countries

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="34%"}
Every subset of training countries scored on each held-out country. The full vocabulary gains about `r f2(Q$tc_slope)` per added training country on the level; the climate-and-soil index starts higher and is positive in `r pc(Q$tcs_pos1)` of single-country fits.
:::
::: {.column width="66%"}
```{r curve, fig.width=5.8, fig.height=4.4, dpi=160}
if (!is.null(TC) && !is.null(TCS)) {
  d <- bind_rows(TC |> filter(arm == "domain_index") |> mutate(set = "Full vocabulary") |> select(target, set, n_train_countries, spearman),
                 TCS |> filter(set == "climate_soil") |> mutate(set = "Climate + soil") |> select(target, set, n_train_countries, spearman)) |>
    group_by(target, set, n_train_countries) |> summarise(mean_rho = mean(spearman, na.rm = TRUE), lo = quantile(spearman, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE), hi = quantile(spearman, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(target = tlab[target])
  ggplot(d, aes(n_train_countries, mean_rho, colour = set)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) + geom_point(size = 3) + geom_linerange(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), alpha = 0.45) +
    facet_wrap(~ target) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:3) + scale_colour_manual(values = c("Full vocabulary" = "#1f4e79", "Climate + soil" = "#b15928")) +
    labs(x = "Training countries", y = "Transported Spearman (mean, IQR)", colour = NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = 13) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
}
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Bars are the interquartile range over fits. Likely question: whether four countries are enough. The curve has not flattened at three training countries, which is the argument for adding surveys to the panel rather than changing the estimator.
:::

## Can the model direct and shrink surveys?

::: {.notes}
What the evidence supports today and what it does not. Supported: with a national anchor (a small nationally representative sample, 5% of a full survey) and the transported climate-and-soil ranking, the median district error is `r f2(Q$ar_a1, 1)` percentage points, which a district-representative survey only matches at about `r pc(Q$ar_b_match)` of the full sample (survey design slide; anchor_and_rank.csv). That is the sample-size claim, and it holds for the LEVEL error only: a district survey of any size captures more burden in its worst fifth, because burden is what it measures directly. In design: model-assisted cluster allocation, where the ranking decides where the clusters go, oversampling the districts the model puts at the top and bottom, so that a survey of the same size resolves the districts that matter; this is designed (CLUSTER_LEVEL_DESIGN_2026-09.md) and not piloted. Not shown: that a proxy model can replace a biomarker survey. The reliability ceiling is the survey\'s own, and the transport correlation of `r f2(Q$tr_index)` is a ranking, not a prevalence. The honest offer to a ministry is: a ranking now from public data, a national anchor to put a level on it, and a district survey designed with the ranking rather than instead of it.
:::

## The dashboard

::: {.notes}
The dashboard was rebuilt on 13 September on the corrected protocol, so that it says exactly what this talk says, simplified on 14 September for a reader with no statistics, and refreshed on 16 September with the 570-layer predictor set that has no DHS in it. Start here now opens with a plain-language abstract (the project, the four training surveys, how the model was built and checked), then the three numbers, one card on how to use the map, and the checklist; the Ghana worked example and the audit history sit in folded panels. Removed with the rebuild: the person-level machine-learning layer (a coin toss under honest folds), the earlier area-level estimators and their intervals, the old leaderboard, the GBD placeholder and the Sierra Leone chiefdom layer. One estimator feeds every tab: the index fitted on all surveyed districts of a country and applied to every district. The chance of being in the worst fifth exists for surveyed districts in three countries; Sierra Leone's 14 districts cannot be cross-validated. A printable brief per country comes from the same tables, and a 25-page static walkthrough of every tab (dashboard_walkthrough_2026-09-14.pdf in the Dropbox folder) is there for written comments. Open items: sharing a view by URL, faster loading (the boundary files are most of the bundle), the worst-fifth probability for unsurveyed districts, and plain-language descriptions for the predictors (75 of 570 have one; the catalogue is the worklist). Open the URL a few minutes before showing it: the free tier stops idle instances and the restart takes a minute.
:::

## Sources, tiers and alignment

```{r source-table}
if (!is.null(MD)) {
  t <- MD |> mutate(Source = source_label(source)) |> group_by(Source) |>
    summarise(Columns = n(), Tier = paste(sort(unique(tier_lab)), collapse = "; "), `Domains` = length(unique(domain)),
              `Year rule` = paste(sort(unique(alignment_rule)), collapse = ", "), `Largest gap (years)` = if (all(is.na(year_offset_max_abs))) "static" else as.character(max(year_offset_max_abs, na.rm = TRUE)), .groups = "drop") |>
    arrange(desc(Columns)) |> mutate(`Year rule` = ifelse(nchar(`Year rule`) > 60, paste0(substr(`Year rule`, 1, 57), "..."), `Year rule`))
  kb(t, digits = 0)
}
```

::: {.notes}
Tier: open means downloadable by anyone; public survey microdata means a registration with the survey programme; DHS means the DHS Program's access agreement. Year rule names are the rule identifiers in metadata/covariates/temporal_alignment.csv. The largest gap is the worst case over the four countries; static layers have none.
:::

## From columns to domains

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="34%"}
`r Q$n_dom` domains. A domain groups columns by what they measure, whatever the source: the MAP, IHME and survey malaria columns sit in one group. Each domain enters the model as its leading principal components, to 80% of variance and at most twelve, learned on the training districts only.
:::
::: {.column width="66%"}
```{r domains, fig.width=6.2, fig.height=5.6, dpi=160}
if (!is.null(MD)) {
  d <- as.data.frame(table(Domain = MD$domain, Tier = MD$tier_lab), stringsAsFactors = FALSE); d <- d[d$Freq > 0, ]
  tot <- tapply(d$Freq, d$Domain, sum); d$Domain <- factor(d$Domain, levels = names(sort(tot))); d$Tier <- factor(d$Tier, levels = names(tier_col))
  ggplot(d, aes(Freq, Domain, fill = Tier)) + geom_col(width = 0.72) +
    geom_text(data = df(Domain = factor(names(tot), levels = levels(d$Domain)), n = as.vector(tot)), aes(n, Domain, label = n), inherit.aes = FALSE, hjust = -0.2, size = 3.2) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = tier_col) + scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) + labs(x = "Columns", y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(), legend.position = "bottom") + guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2))
}
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Why domains: `r Q$n` columns against 14 to 87 districts per country cannot be fitted column by column, and the columns are heavily correlated within a source. Grouping them by what they measure and taking principal components inside each group keeps most of the variance of each group, treats a source with 64 columns and a source with 3 as one construct each, and keeps the outcome out of the representation: the rotations are learned from the training districts' predictors alone, so nothing is selected on the biomarker. The grouping is written down: each source block brings a label, and `r if (!is.null(OV)) nrow(OV) else 10` override rules in metadata/covariates/domain_overrides.csv regroup columns by construct (infection and inflammation burden, immunisation, anaemia, child anthropometry, infant feeding, supplementation, water and sanitation, education, child mortality, assets), so that MAP, IHME, DHS and MICS versions of the same thing are weighed together. Two things went wrong this week and are now guarded. A domain's first twelve characters are its key inside the model; two labels that shared them ("Food prices (RTFP)" and "Food prices and supply") were silently merged in two analyses until a check caught it on 16 September. The other is in the exclusions, on the next slide. One more point for questions: climate alone or soil alone transports better than all domains together, the analysis deck's climate-and-soil result.
:::

## The twenty layers behind child iron, and how much each carries

```{r twenty-iron, fig.width=11, fig.height=6.4, dpi=170}
if (!is.null(IT)) {
  d <- IT |> filter(outcome == "child_iron", target == "level", rank <= 20) |>
    mutate(name = ifelse(is.na(PLAIN[column]), clean_code(column), unname(PLAIN[column])),
           lab = sprintf("%.1f%%%s", 100 * share, ifelse(incountry_sign_agree == incountry_fits, "  *", "")), name = factor(name, levels = rev(name)))
  doms <- sort(unique(d$domain)); pal <- c("#1f4e79", "#6baed6", "#8c510a", "#33a02c", "#b15928", "#6a3d9a", "#e08214", "#0F7B8A", "#cab2d6", "#fdbf6f", "#d7191c", "#9e9ac8", "#7fcdbb", "#fdae61")
  ggplot(d, aes(beta_std, name, fill = domain)) + geom_col(width = 0.72) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey40") +
    geom_text(aes(label = lab, x = ifelse(beta_std > 0, beta_std + 0.1, beta_std - 0.1), hjust = ifelse(beta_std > 0, 0, 1)), size = 3.3, colour = "grey30") +
    scale_fill_manual(values = stats::setNames(rep(pal, length.out = length(doms)), doms)) + scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = 0.18)) +
    labs(x = "Standardised weight in the pooled index (left: district ranks better; right: worse)
Label: share of the index carried; * = same direction in each country's own fit", y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.text = element_text(size = 9), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), axis.title.x = element_text(size = 9.5)) + guides(fill = guide_legend(ncol = 3, byrow = TRUE))
}
```

::: {.notes}
index_importance_top.csv, child iron, biomarker level: the twenty largest standardised weights in the pooled four-country fit, drawn as bars so their sizes can be compared. The level target is the negated log ferritin, so a bar to the right means districts with more of the layer rank worse on child iron, to the left better. The label is the share of the index's variance the layer carries: the twenty together hold about a fifth of the index (`r if (!is.null(IT)) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * sum(IT$share[IT$outcome == "child_iron" & IT$target == "level" & IT$rank <= 20])) else "21%"`), the rest is spread over the other 350 columns, which is how a weighted sum of many weak signals is meant to behave. All twenty keep their direction in every leave-one-country-out fit; the starred ones (`r if (!is.null(IT)) sum(IT$incountry_sign_agree[IT$outcome == "child_iron" & IT$target == "level" & IT$rank <= 20] == IT$incountry_fits[IT$outcome == "child_iron" & IT$target == "level" & IT$rank <= 20]) else 10` of twenty) also keep it in each country's own separate fit, the stricter test. The story is the one on the earlier slides: cereal-heavy cropping, ruminant and cattle density, cropland, distance from the coast and a high dependency ratio rank a district worse; root crops, higher plant productivity, relatively expensive staples, modelled overweight and malaria intensity rank it better, the last for the geographic reason discussed. None of the twenty requires a blood sample, and the twenty-layer equal-weight composite scores about the same as the full index for a new country.
:::

## Exclusions, with their reasons

```{r exclusions}
if (!is.null(EX)) {
  e <- EX |> transmute(Rule = canonical_regex, Policy = policy, Reason = ifelse(nchar(reason) > 110, paste0(substr(reason, 1, 107), "..."), reason))
  kb(e, digits = 0)
}
```

::: {.notes}
metadata/covariates/exclusions.csv, applied by scripts/protocol_v2/53_apply_exclusion_policy.R to the live set. Data defects are removed on evidence in the audit tables; superseded layers are replaced by a better-aligned version of the same quantity; redundant twins are removed when a pooled rank correlation reaches 0.98 with a kept column. The two soil rules that failed that standard were removed on 15 September (SX-01 in the sandbox log).
:::

## Predictor set by domain and tier

```{r domain-table}
if (!is.null(MD)) {
  t <- MD |> group_by(Domain = domain) |> summarise(Columns = n(), `Open` = sum(tier == "open"), `Public microdata` = sum(tier == "survey_public"), `DHS` = sum(tier == "survey_dhs"),
                                                    `Vary within country` = sum(subn), `Modelled surfaces` = sum(as.logical(toupper(as.character(modelled_surface))), na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |> arrange(desc(Columns))
  kb(t, digits = 0)
}
```

::: {.notes}
Modelled surfaces are estimates produced by someone else's model (IHME, MAP, the MIMI dietary inadequacy estimates); they are included by default and the protocol has a switch (V2_DROP_MODELLED=1) to score without them. Columns that do not vary within a country are the national constants dropped at fit time.
:::

## What we would add next, and the rule for adding it

- Sub-national household-survey microdata with GPS: MICS cluster coordinates for Ghana 2017-18 and Malawi 2013-14 are requested; they turn region-level blocks into district ones.
- Diet from the household budget surveys for Ghana (GLSS7 food module) and Sierra Leone (SLIHS diary codes), so the 15 diet indicators cover all four countries.
- Conflict events (ACLED, four-country export), market prices for Ghana and Sierra Leone, a decision on FluNet's national counts.
- Every candidate block passes the same test before it enters: within-country sign agreement, paired in-fill with and without it, and leave-one-country-out.

::: {.notes}
The add-on harness is scripts/protocol_v2/39_addon_feature_test.R and it has scored eleven blocks so far; the analysis deck's forest plot of those tests is the record. Most recent blocks moved the index by less than 0.01. The household budget survey block and the MICS block are in the base set for what they add inside a country, where two of the three estimands live; they do not help across borders. The GPS request is with UNICEF; the Ghana and Sierra Leone budget-survey modules are with the research assistant. Cote d'Ivoire, the country we rank with no survey, is missing the 30-year climate normals, which cost 27 of the 101 climate-and-soil columns in its intersection without changing the transport figure; extracting them is a morning's work.
:::

## Predictors recurring across outcomes

```{r importance-patterns}
if (!is.null(IP)) {
  d <- IP |> filter(target == "level", outcomes_in_top20 >= 3) |> arrange(desc(outcomes_in_top20), mean_rank) |> head(12) |>
    transmute(Predictor = column, Domain = domain, `Outcomes (top 20)` = outcomes_in_top20, Signs = signs, `Mean rank` = mean_rank)
  kb(d, digits = 1)
}
```

::: {.notes}
Predictors in the pooled top 20 of three or more of the six outcomes on the level target, with the sign in each. One gradient recurs: districts that are drier and grassier, less productive (lower net and gross primary productivity), more pastoral, poorer (less home ownership, fewer women in paid work, less schooling) and more stunted rank worse on every deficiency. Outcome-specific signals sit below it: haemoglobin C allele frequency and cattle for child iron, the modelled anaemia surfaces for women's iron, helminth treatment coverage and the drought index for folate, elevation and coast distance for B12.
:::

## Weighting of the domain components

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="34%"}
Alternative weightings of the same components on the biomarker level. In-country every joint fit loses to the marginal-correlation weights (ridge `r sgn(Q$wsi_ridge)`, elastic net `r sgn(Q$wsi_enet)`, lasso `r sgn(Q$wsi_lasso)`). Across borders the decorrelated index gains `r sgn(Q$ws_decor["d"], 3)` (better in `r Q$ws_decor["b"]` of `r Q$ws_decor["n"]`).
:::
::: {.column width="66%"}
```{r weights, fig.width=5.8, fig.height=5.2, dpi=160}
if (!is.null(WS)) {
  lab <- c(domain_index = "Production index (pooled rank correlation)", index_soft1 = "Soft threshold, |z| < 1 to zero", index_decor = "Decorrelated across domains",
           index_meta = "Replication-weighted (meta z)", ridge_min = "Ridge, inner CV", ridge_nested = "Ridge, nested block CV on rank",
           domain_enet = "Elastic net, inner CV", enet_1se = "Elastic net, one-SE rule", lasso_min = "Lasso, inner CV", sparse20 = "Top 20 predictors, equal weights")
  d <- WS |> filter(target == "level", arm %in% names(lab)) |> cell_ci("spearman", c("estimand", "arm")) |>
    mutate(Model = factor(lab[arm], levels = rev(lab)), Estimand = factor(c(infill = "In-fill", region = "Region", country = "Transport")[estimand], levels = c("In-fill", "Region", "Transport")))
  forest(d, "Model", facet = "Estimand", null = 0, base = 12)
}
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
The production weights are the infinite-penalty limit of a ridge regression on the components, so the rows are points along that family plus other sources of evidence for the weights (soft thresholding, meta-analytic replication across training countries, decorrelation across domains). Same folds and cells as every other arm; five in-fill draws. The one-SE rules return the null model in some cells (`r Q$ws_1se_scored` of `r Q$tr_cells` transport cells scored for the elastic net). The twenty-predictor composite gains `r sgn(Q$ws_sparse20["d"], 3)` across borders (better in `r Q$ws_sparse20["b"]` of `r Q$ws_sparse20["n"]`) and costs `r sgn(Q$wsi_sparse20)` in-fill. The soft threshold gained 0.02 across borders on the direct DHS estimates and `r sgn(Q$ws_soft1["d"], 3)` on the smoothed ones, so that gain was a property of noisy inputs. Both gains were found among 21 arms on these cells and are pre-registered for the next country rather than adopted. Prevalence-target version in the appendix.
:::

## Sparse composites

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="34%"}
Equal-weight composites of the top 5, 10 and 20 predictors, membership chosen inside each training fold by back-projected index weight. Twenty predictors cost `r sgn(Q$wsi_sparse20)` in-fill and gain `r sgn(Q$ws_sparse20["d"], 3)` across borders; five predictors cost `r sgn(Q$wsi_sparse5)` in-fill.
:::
::: {.column width="66%"}
```{r sparse, fig.width=5.8, fig.height=4.2, dpi=160}
if (!is.null(WS)) {
  lab <- c(domain_index = "Full index", sparse20 = "Top 20, equal weights", sparse10 = "Top 10, equal weights", sparse10w = "Top 10, index weights", sparse5 = "Top 5, equal weights")
  d <- WS |> filter(target == "level", arm %in% names(lab)) |> cell_ci("spearman", c("estimand", "arm")) |>
    mutate(Model = factor(lab[arm], levels = rev(lab)), Estimand = factor(c(infill = "In-fill", region = "Region", country = "Transport")[estimand], levels = c("In-fill", "Region", "Transport")))
  forest(d, "Model", facet = "Estimand", null = 0, base = 13)
}
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Dawes' improper linear model: direction from the training fold, equal weights, rescaled like the index; nothing is chosen on held-out districts. Weighting the ten by their index weights instead of equally changes nothing. The composite is a transport and communication tool: twenty public layers a ministry can compute. Likely question: which twenty. The next slide lists the child iron members.
:::

## Child iron composite

```{r sparse-members}
if (!is.null(IT) && !is.null(MD)) {
  d <- IT |> filter(outcome == "child_iron", target == "level", rank <= 20) |> arrange(rank) |> left_join(MD[, c("column", "source")], by = "column") |>
    transmute(rank, p = paste0(column, " (", ifelse(beta > 0, "+", "-"), ")"), src = sub(" [(].*$", "", source))
  kb(data.frame(Predictor = d$p[1:10], Source = d$src[1:10], `Predictor ` = d$p[11:20], `Source ` = d$src[11:20], check.names = FALSE), digits = 0)
}
```

::: {.notes}
The twenty columns the four-country fit would deploy for child iron, in order of weight, with the sign of the contribution (plus means more deficiency). `r Q$ci_loco` of the twenty keep their sign in every leave-one-country-out fit and `r Q$ci_rep` in every country's own independent fit. In the benchmark the membership is re-chosen inside each training fold; this is the version fitted on all four countries. The other outcomes' composites are in results/tables/protocol_v2/index_importance_top.csv.
:::

## Urbanicity conditioning

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="34%"}
Transported Spearman of the climate-and-soil index at district level (`r f2(Q$ur_cs)`), the same after partialling out an urbanicity composite (`r f2(Q$ur_partial)`), and urbanicity alone (`r f2(Q$ur_only)`).
:::
::: {.column width="66%"}
```{r urban, fig.width=5.8, fig.height=4.0, dpi=160}
if (!is.null(UR)) {
  d <- UR |> filter(target == "level") |> transmute(tier = ifelse(tier == "admin1", "Regional", "District"), outcome, heldout, `Climate + soil index` = rho_cs, `Partialling out urbanicity` = partial_cs, `Urbanicity alone` = rho_urb_only) |>
    pivot_longer(c(`Climate + soil index`, `Partialling out urbanicity`, `Urbanicity alone`), names_to = "quantity", values_to = "v") |> cell_ci("v", c("tier", "quantity")) |>
    mutate(quantity = factor(quantity, levels = rev(c("Climate + soil index", "Partialling out urbanicity", "Urbanicity alone"))))
  forest(d, "quantity", facet = "tier", null = 0, base = 13)
}
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Urbanicity composite: night lights, population density, built surface, urban land cover, travel time to health care. The replicated associations (legumes, cattle, soil chemistry, night-time temperature, all toward more deficiency) describe where subsistence agriculture is, so an urban-rural gradient was the rival explanation; partialling it out moves the transported correlation by less than 0.02 and urbanicity alone does not transport.
:::

## Add-on predictor blocks

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="34%"}
Median change in Spearman when a block is added to the base vocabulary, in-fill and district transport on the biomarker level, scored under one harness with the same folds.
:::
::: {.column width="66%"}
```{r addons, fig.width=5.8, fig.height=4.8, dpi=160}
tags <- c(food_tm = "Food prices, fieldwork-matched", climate_tm = "Temperature and rainfall, fieldwork-matched", alphaearth = "Satellite embedding as own domain",
          livestock = "Livestock density", water_distance = "Distance to water and coast", espen = "Helminth burden and control", ihme_raster = "IHME surfaces as zonal means",
          fe_clim_aw = "Engineered climatology", fe_terrain_aw = "Terrain", fe_soil_aw = "Soil bioavailability")
rows <- lapply(names(tags), function(t) { i <- rd(P2, paste0("addon_", t, "_infill.csv")); l <- rd(P2, paste0("addon_", t, "_loco.csv")); if (is.null(i) || is.null(l)) return(NULL)
  di <- i |> filter(target == "level") |> group_by(country, outcome) |> summarise(d = mean(spearman[set == "plus"], na.rm = TRUE) - mean(spearman[set == "base"], na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
  dl <- l |> filter(tier == "admin2", target == "level") |> group_by(heldout, outcome) |> summarise(d = mean(spearman[set == "plus"], na.rm = TRUE) - mean(spearman[set == "base"], na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
  bind_rows(df(Block = tags[[t]], Estimand = "In-fill", d = di$d), df(Block = tags[[t]], Estimand = "Transport", d = dl$d)) })
rows <- bind_rows(rows[!sapply(rows, is.null)])
if (nrow(rows)) {
  d <- rows |> group_by(Block, Estimand) |> summarise(est = median(d, na.rm = TRUE), lo = quantile(d, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE), hi = quantile(d, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
  ord <- d |> filter(Estimand == "Transport") |> arrange(est); d$Block <- factor(d$Block, levels = ord$Block)
  ggplot(d, aes(est, Block)) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey45") + geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), width = 0.25, colour = "grey35", orientation = "y") +
    geom_point(size = 3, colour = "#1f4e79") + facet_wrap(~ Estimand) + labs(x = "Change in Spearman when the block is added (median, IQR over cells)", y = NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
}
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Bars are the interquartile range over cells. No block moves in-fill or transport by more than 0.01 at the median: the vocabulary is saturated. The fieldwork-matched temperature columns are among the most consistently associated with deficiency in the marginal scan yet improve no fold, because a covariate defined by when the survey happened cannot rank districts that have not been surveyed. Found in passing and fixed: the price columns used 2021 as The Gambia's survey year (fieldwork was January to April 2018), and the satellite embedding had been filed under agriculture.
:::

## Cluster-level fitting

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="34%"}
The same index fitted at the survey cluster and aggregated to districts, against the district fit, on the same cells. In-fill on the level: `r f2(Q$cv_agg)` cluster-fitted against `r f2(Q$cv_dist)` district-fitted.
:::
::: {.column width="66%"}
```{r cluster, fig.width=5.8, fig.height=4.2, dpi=160}
if (!is.null(CV)) {
  d <- CV |> filter(set == "transportable", arm == "domain_index") |> transmute(estimand = c(infill = "In-fill", region = "Region")[estimand], target = tlab[target], country, outcome, `Cluster-fitted, aggregated to districts` = rho_agg, `District-fitted` = rho_district_v2) |>
    pivot_longer(c(`Cluster-fitted, aggregated to districts`, `District-fitted`), names_to = "fit", values_to = "v") |> cell_ci("v", c("estimand", "target", "fit")) |>
    mutate(panel = paste(estimand, target, sep = ", "), fit = factor(fit, levels = rev(c("District-fitted", "Cluster-fitted, aggregated to districts"))))
  forest(d, "fit", facet = "panel", null = 0, base = 12)
}
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
`r Q$n_clusters` clusters with GPS; covariates as 2 km (urban) and 5 km (rural) buffer means from rasters on disk; the same estimands with folds cut by district and region. Cluster-fitted models trail district-fitted ones on every estimand and for transport. A precision-weighted index and empirical-Bayes shrinkage of cluster outcomes recover a third to a half of the gap. A matched-vocabulary comparison attributes the remaining gap to the layers rather than the fitting unit. The cluster track is a sensitivity analysis until its vocabulary is matched layer for layer.
:::

## Risk-class accuracy

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="34%"}
Share of districts placed in the correct WHO vitamin A band (under 2%, 2 to 10, 10 to 20, 20 or more), and within one band, mean over the vitamin A cells. The index in-fill: `r pc(Q$rc_ex)` exact and `r pc(Q$rc_w1)` within one band.
:::
::: {.column width="66%"}
```{r riskcat, fig.width=5.8, fig.height=4.4, dpi=160}
if (!is.null(RC)) {
  lab <- c(domain_index = "Zero-tuning index, in-fill", spatial_plus_domain = "Smoother + covariates, in-fill", spatial = "Spatial smoother, in-fill", region_mean_jk = "Jackknifed regional mean, in-fill",
           transport_anchored_full = "Transport, full index + national anchor", transport_anchored_climate_soil = "Transport, climate + soil + national anchor")
  d <- RC |> filter(scheme == "who_vitA", arm %in% names(lab)) |> transmute(country, outcome, arm, `Exact band` = exact_admin2, `Within one band` = within1_admin2) |>
    pivot_longer(c(`Exact band`, `Within one band`), names_to = "measure", values_to = "v") |> cell_ci("v", c("arm", "measure")) |> mutate(Model = factor(lab[arm], levels = rev(lab)))
  forest(d, "Model", facet = "measure", null = NA_real_, base = 12, xlab = "Share of districts (mean, 95% interval)") + scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent)
}
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Out-of-fold predictions averaged over ten draws; transport rows use the held-out country's own national prevalence as the anchor (AR-01 design), the only honest way to put a transported ranking on the prevalence scale. The January deck's child vitamin A cell was 44 and 75 percent (exact, within one) for the full model from the old leaderboard. For iron and the other outcomes only the 20 percent threshold has a WHO source; the two-class accuracies are in results/tables/protocol_v2/risk_category_accuracy_summary.csv.
:::

## LSMS and FluNet predictors

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="34%"}
Ghana in-fill on the biomarker level with the base vocabulary, the base plus the LSMS block, and the LSMS block alone, median over ten draws.
:::
::: {.column width="66%"}
```{r lsms, fig.width=5.8, fig.height=4.2, dpi=160}
if (!is.null(LI)) {
  d <- LI |> filter(country == "Ghana", target == "level", set %in% c("base", "plus", "addon_only")) |> group_by(outcome, set) |> summarise(rho = median(spearman, na.rm = TRUE), lo = quantile(spearman, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE), hi = quantile(spearman, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(Outcome = olab[outcome], Set = factor(c(base = "Base vocabulary", plus = "Base + LSMS", addon_only = "LSMS alone")[set], levels = c("Base vocabulary", "Base + LSMS", "LSMS alone")))
  ggplot(d, aes(rho, Outcome, colour = Set)) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey45") + geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), width = 0.25, orientation = "y", position = position_dodge(width = 0.6)) +
    geom_point(size = 3, position = position_dodge(width = 0.6)) + scale_colour_manual(values = c("Base vocabulary" = "#1f4e79", "Base + LSMS" = "#b15928", "LSMS alone" = "grey50")) +
    labs(x = "Spearman (median, IQR over draws)", y = NULL, colour = NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = 13) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
}
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
The LSMS block scored here is Ghana's GLSS7 as a svyby object: 134 region-level household expenditure and asset means, broadcast to districts through the 16-to-10 region crosswalk, so the block varies only across ten regions. It does not improve any Ghana cell beyond noise and cannot be scored across borders. The household budget surveys now enter the base set another way, as diet and consumption indicators computed from the microdata for all four countries (GLSS7 for Ghana, again at the region); that block is part of the base vocabulary this slide compares against. FluNet reports for Ghana and Sierra Leone only and is a national weekly count, constant within a country; it contributes nothing by construction.
:::

## Individual-level models

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="34%"}
Person-level SuperLearner under district-blocked folds, Brier skill over the national prevalence, by country and outcome. Mean AUC over `r Q$il_cells` cells: `r f2(Q$il_auc_s)` for survey variables, `r f2(Q$il_auc_p)` for district proxies, `r f2(Q$il_auc_b)` for both.
:::
::: {.column width="66%"}
```{r individual, fig.width=5.8, fig.height=4.6, dpi=160}
if (!is.null(IL) && nrow(IL)) {
  d <- IL |> mutate(Outcome = olab[outcome], set = factor(c(survey_only = "Survey variables only", proxies_only = "District proxies only", both = "Both")[set], levels = c("Survey variables only", "District proxies only", "Both")), country = sub("SierraLeone", "Sierra Leone", country))
  ggplot(d, aes(x = 100 * brier_skill, y = Outcome, colour = set)) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") + geom_point(size = 2.6, position = position_dodge(width = 0.5)) +
    facet_wrap(~ country, nrow = 1) + scale_colour_manual(values = c("Survey variables only" = "#1f4e79", "District proxies only" = "#b15928", "Both" = "grey45")) +
    labs(x = "Brier skill over the national prevalence (%)", y = NULL, colour = NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
}
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Library: mean, elastic net, random forest; survey weights; inner folds blocked by district; outer 5-fold by district so no district's respondents are split across training and test. Survey variables: up to 80 respondent columns with 70 percent coverage after removing biomarkers, adjustments, identifiers, weights, dates and locations. Proxies: the district's domain components joined to each respondent. Person-level skill exists for iron only (survey-variable AUC up to `r f2(Q$il_iron_max)` in Ghana and Malawi); vitamin A, folate and B12 show none. The January figure (Brier skill 20 to 60 percent) came from folds not blocked by district and a survey set that included biomarker-adjacent variables. Aggregating a person-level classifier biases area means, so this remains a sensitivity analysis. Rerun on the RR-10 set on 10 September.
:::

## National-level track

```{r national}
if (!is.null(NE)) { d <- NE |> filter(model_type == "binary", outcome %in% c("child_vitA", "women_vitA", "child_iron", "women_iron")) |> group_by(Outcome = olab[outcome]) |>
  summarise(Countries = dplyr::n(), `Observed (mean)` = mean(obs_prev), `Predicted (mean)` = mean(pred_prev), `Mean absolute error (pp)` = 100 * mean(abs_diff), .groups = "drop"); kb(d, digits = 2) }
```

The January deck's national-level track (WHO VMNIS and BRINDA outcomes, FAOSTAT and policy predictors) lives in a separate sub-pipeline last run in April 2026. It is not part of the current protocol and has not been re-audited; the table is its last output for the four survey countries. It is the only track with time series and fortification policy indicators and is a candidate for a rerun under the corrected protocol.
:::

## Iodine

```{r iodine}
if (!is.null(IO)) { d <- IO |> filter(analysis == "protocol") |> mutate(cell = paste0(ifelse(country == "Gambia", "Gambia ", "Sierra Leone "), ifelse(target == "p_low", "UIC < 100", "median UIC"), ", ", ifelse(estimand == "infill", "in-fill", "region")),
    Model = c(null_train_mean = "Training mean", region_mean_jk = "Jackknifed regional mean", spatial = "Spatial smoother", domain_index = "Zero-tuning index", spatial_plus_domain = "Smoother + covariates")[arm]) |>
    select(Model, cell, spearman) |> pivot_wider(names_from = cell, values_from = spearman) |> mutate(across(-Model, ~ ifelse(is.finite(.x), sprintf("%.2f", .x), "-"))); kb(d, digits = 2) }
```

::: {.notes}
Urinary iodine is measured in The Gambia (continuous, with household salt iodine) and in Sierra Leone (six WHO categories, non-lactating women); it left the modelling outcomes because a one- or two-country outcome has no leave-one-country-out test. Targets: district prevalence of urinary iodine concentration below 100 micrograms per litre and, for The Gambia, the district median. In-fill needs at least 15 districts, so it runs for The Gambia only; leave-one-region-out runs in both. Whether district salt iodisation tracks district iodine status is in results/tables/protocol_v2/iodine_in_country.csv (rows analysis = descriptive).
:::

## Weighting of the domain components: prevalence

```{r weights-prev, fig.width=10, fig.height=5.0, dpi=140}
if (!is.null(WS)) {
  lab <- c(domain_index = "Production index (pooled rank correlation)", index_soft1 = "Soft threshold, |z| < 1 to zero", index_decor = "Decorrelated across domains",
           index_meta = "Replication-weighted (meta z)", ridge_min = "Ridge, inner CV", ridge_nested = "Ridge, nested block CV on rank",
           domain_enet = "Elastic net, inner CV", enet_1se = "Elastic net, one-SE rule", lasso_min = "Lasso, inner CV", sparse20 = "Top 20 predictors, equal weights")
  d <- WS |> filter(target == "prev", arm %in% names(lab)) |> cell_ci("spearman", c("estimand", "arm")) |>
    mutate(Model = factor(lab[arm], levels = rev(lab)), Estimand = factor(c(infill = "In-fill", region = "Region", country = "Transport")[estimand], levels = c("In-fill", "Region", "Transport")))
  forest(d, "Model", facet = "Estimand", null = 0, base = 13)
}
```

::: {.notes}
Prevalence target, same arms and folds as the biomarker-level figure. Mean Spearman over cells with a 95% interval across cells.
:::

## Geostatistical comparator: absolute error

```{r geostat-wmae, fig.width=10, fig.height=4.6, dpi=140}
if (!is.null(MBG)) {
  lab <- c(domain_index = "Zero-tuning domain index", mbg = "Geostatistical, field + domain covariates", mbg_dhs = "Geostatistical, field + DHS covariate list", mbg_gp = "Geostatistical, field only", spatial = "Spatial smoother", region_mean_jk = "Jackknifed regional mean")
  d <- MBG |> filter(estimand == "infill", target == "prev", arm %in% names(lab)) |> cell_ci("wmae_agg", "arm") |> mutate(Model = factor(lab[arm], levels = rev(lab)))
  forest(d, "Model", null = NA_real_, base = 14, xlab = "Weighted mean absolute error, percentage points (mean, 95% interval)")
}
```

::: {.notes}
In-fill, prevalence. The geostatistical model estimates a level and shrinks uncertain districts toward the mean, which lowers absolute error; the index ranks and is rescaled to the training outcome's spread, which does not. If the deliverable is a prevalence figure for a named district, the geostatistical model is the right tool; if it is a ranking, the index is.
:::

::: {.notes}
The individual-level SuperLearner remains a sensitivity analysis because shrinking a noisy individual classifier biases area means; it was removed from the dashboard on 13 September, which now shows only the protocol's index (amertens.shinyapps.io/micronutrient-burden).
:::
